reason: The passage names several characters who are not leaders. Most prominently, Hannah (חַנָּה) is a central named figure throughout this passage, yet she is described as one of Elkanah's wives, notably barren and provoked by her rival. She is not a leader. Similarly, Peninnah (פְּנִנָּה), Elkanah's second wife, is named but holds no leadership position. While Eli (עֵלִי), Hophni (חָפְנִי), and Phineas (פִּנְחָס) are priests (religious leaders), and Elkanah is a patriarch, Hannah and Peninnah are explicitly non-leadership figures. Samuel (שְׁמוּאֵל), though named, is merely an infant in this passage and not yet a leader. The passage's narrative focus on Hannah's barrenness, prayer, and personal struggle makes it clear that named characters include non-leadership figures.
